warmup.q: A JDK proxy for interface Scenes { int minutes(String s); default int total(String a, String b) { return minutes(a) + minutes(b); } } has a handler that logs each call and then does return method.invoke(target, args);. A caller runs proxy.total("prologue", "duel"). How many calls does the handler log?
options: 2: minutes twice, because default methods never reach the handler
warmup.why: total reaches the handler like any interface method. The handler then runs the default body on the target, where this is the target, so the two minutes calls never pass through the proxy. Run the body with InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, args) instead, and this is the proxy: the handler then logs 3 calls. The section on default methods shows both runs.

opening:
Picture a busy lead actor with a stand-in at the stage door. Every request meant for the actor goes to the stand-in first: a costume fitting, a photo, a note from the director. The stand-in writes each one down, tries again if the actor doesn't answer, and then passes it on. The actor's work doesn't change at all. The extra jobs happen at the door.

Java can put a stand-in like that in front of any interface, while your program runs. java.lang.reflect.Proxy writes a new class on the spot, and every call on it goes to one method of yours, an InvocationHandler. You met the pattern in Decorator and Proxy. In the last lesson, call sites linked to methods that already existed; this time the JDK writes a whole class.

The one-line handler, "pass every call on", looks finished after the first test. It quietly breaks equals, wraps exceptions twice, and retries steps that already worked. In this lesson, we'll build a stand-in by hand, read the class the JDK writes, sort out what the handler owes its callers, and decide who this is inside a default method. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a stand-in at the stage door who takes every request for an actor, does a little extra, and passes it on. The JDK builds that stand-in as a real class, and every call becomes one invoke. The handler must answer equals for itself and unwrap exceptions, and invokeDefault makes this the proxy.

Now search your code for InvocationHandler or newProxyInstance, and check each handler for the four cases: Object methods, default methods, the real work, and an unwrapping catch.

Next, we'll stand in front of classes that have no interface at all. How do tools such as Byte Buddy, and frameworks such as Spring and Quarkus, build a stand-in by writing a subclass?

sections.h: Building a stand-in by hand, then reading the one the JDK writes
sections.html:
The show program asks the theatre's wardrobe system how many costumes each role has. It talks to it through a small interface, Wardrobe, with one method, costumes(role), and a default method dressed(role) that checks the count is above 0. (A default method is an interface method that has a body.)

Let's first write a stand-in by hand, for this one interface. It holds one InvocationHandler: an object with a single method, invoke(proxy, method, args), that receives every call. In the theatre picture, the proxy object is the stand-in, and the handler is the rule the stand-in follows for every request. The real object behind it all, the actor, is called the target. Each request arrives as one note: which method was called (a java.lang.reflect.Method, the object that describes a method) and its arguments, in an Object[]:

Java
final class HandProxy implements Wardrobe {
    private static final Method COSTUMES;                       // 1. looked up once
    static {
        try {
            COSTUMES = Wardrobe.class.getMethod("costumes", String.class);
        } catch (NoSuchMethodException e) {
            throw new NoSuchMethodError(e.getMessage());
        }
    }

    private final InvocationHandler h;
    HandProxy(InvocationHandler h) { this.h = h; }

    @Override
    public int costumes(String role) {
        try {
            return (Integer) h.invoke(this, COSTUMES, new Object[]{role});   // 2. box, ask the handler, unbox
        } catch (RuntimeException | Error e) {
            throw e;                                                      // 3. unchecked: as is
        } catch (Throwable t) {
            throw new UndeclaredThrowableException(t);                    // 4. undeclared checked: wrapped
        }
    }
    // ...the same for dressed, equals, hashCode and toString
}
Kotlin
class HandProxy(private val h: InvocationHandler) : KWardrobe {
    override fun costumes(role: String): Int =
        try {
            h.invoke(this, COSTUMES, arrayOf(role)) as Int               // 2. box, ask the handler, unbox
        } catch (e: RuntimeException) {
            throw e                                                    // 3. unchecked: as is
        } catch (e: Error) {
            throw e
        } catch (t: Throwable) {
            throw UndeclaredThrowableException(t)                      // 4. undeclared checked: wrapped
        }
    // ...the same for dressed, equals, hashCode and toString

    companion object {
        private val COSTUMES = KWardrobe::class.java.getMethod("costumes", String::class.java)  // 1. once
    }
}

Each method finds its Method object once and puts the arguments into an Object[]. Boxing turns primitive values such as int into objects such as Integer along the way. Then it asks the handler and unboxes the answer. That compiles and works: a test with a handler that always answers 3 printed 3. Writing it by hand for forty methods on six interfaces is the kind of job nobody volunteers for twice, so the JDK writes it for you.

In Decorator and Proxy you passed a handler to Proxy.newProxyInstance. At that moment the JDK generated a class like HandProxy, for whichever interfaces you listed. Here's what ProxyAnatomy reports about it, on JDK 21 and JDK 25 alike:

class      public final jdk.proxy1.$Proxy0
extends    java.lang.reflect.Proxy, implements [interface ...ProxyAnatomy$Wardrobe]
module     jdk.proxy1, hidden: false
fields     [m0, m1, m2, m3, m4]
methods    [costumes, dressed, equals, hashCode, proxyClassLookup, toString]

The Proxy Javadoc promises most of this. A proxy class is final, extends java.lang.reflect.Proxy, and implements exactly the interfaces you passed, in the same order. Its name isn't specified, but names that start with $Proxy are kept for proxy classes, and Proxy.isProxyClass recognizes it. The module jdk.proxy1 and the counter in $Proxy0 are details of the JDK, free to change.

Every generated method looks like HandProxy.costumes, written straight in bytecode. This is costumes(String) as JDK 25 generated it:

public final int costumes(java.lang.String) throws ;      // JDK 25, names shortened
   0: aload_0
   1: getfield      Proxy.h:InvocationHandler                   // 1. the handler
   4: aload_0                                                    // 2. the proxy itself
   5: getstatic     m3:Method                                    // 3. Method looked up once, in <clinit>
   8: iconst_1
   9: anewarray     Object                                       // 4. box the arguments into an Object[]
  12: dup
  13: iconst_0
  14: aload_1
  15: aastore
  16: invokeinterface InvocationHandler.invoke:(Object;Method;[Object;)Object
  21: checkcast     Integer                                      // 5. unbox the result
  24: invokevirtual Integer.intValue:()I
  27: ireturn
  28: athrow                                                     // Error, RuntimeException: rethrow as is
  29: new           UndeclaredThrowableException                 // anything else: wrap it
  ...
Exception table:
   from  to  target  type
     0   28    28    Class java/lang/Error
     0   28    28    Class java/lang/RuntimeException
     0   28    29    any

So every call loads the handler and the proxy, and fetches the Method object that the static initializer looked up once. (m0 to m2 are hashCode, equals and toString, then come your interface's methods.) It copies the arguments into a fresh Object[] and calls invoke. The result is cast back and unboxed. A null returned for a primitive return type becomes a NullPointerException at that unboxing step.

The exception table, the list at the end of a method that says which instructions each catch guards, is the whole exception contract. Error and RuntimeException pass straight through, and so do checked exceptions that the interface method declares. Anything else gets wrapped in UndeclaredThrowableException. costumes declares nothing, so its last entry is any.

The Kotlin twin prints the same shape for a Kotlin interface. Proxies are a JVM feature, and kotlinc's interfaces are ordinary JVM interfaces. Since JDK 23, the JDK writes these classes with the ClassFile API. JDK 21 still used its internal copy of ASM, a library for writing class files, so its bytecode differs slightly in the exception handler.

A JDK proxy turns every call into one invoke with a Method and an Object[].

Every call, then, lands in one place. Which calls, exactly, and what must the handler hand back?

try.title: Take a proxy apart
steps: Read ProxyAnatomy (or ProxyAnatomy.kt). Before running it, predict which of the five calls in part 2 reach the handler.
Run it. Check the class name, its fields and methods, and the list the handler saw.
Look at part 3: why do {Wardrobe, Audited} and {Audited, Wardrobe} get different class names?

code.title: ProxyAnatomy.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l04; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler; import java.lang.reflect.Modifier; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; /** What Proxy.newProxyInstance generates, which calls reach the handler, and how the class is cached. */ public class ProxyAnatomy { public interface Wardrobe { int costumes(String role); default boolean dressed(String role) { return costumes(role) > 0; } } public interface Audited { String auditId(); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> seen = new ArrayList<>(); InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, a) -> { seen.add(m.getDeclaringClass().getSimpleName() + "." + m.getName()); return switch (m.getName()) { case "costumes" -> 3; case "hashCode" -> 42; case "equals" -> proxy == a[0]; case "toString" -> "Wardrobe proxy"; default -> null; }; }; ClassLoader app = Wardrobe.class.getClassLoader(); Wardrobe q = (Wardrobe) Proxy.newProxyInstance(app, new Class<?>[]{Wardrobe.class}, h); // 1. the generated class Class<?> pc = q.getClass(); System.out.println("class " + Modifier.toString(pc.getModifiers()) + " " + pc.getName()); System.out.println("extends " + pc.getSuperclass().getName() + ", implements " + Arrays.toString(pc.getInterfaces())); System.out.println("module " + pc.getModule().getName() + ", hidden: " + pc.isHidden()); System.out.println("fields " + Arrays.stream(pc.getDeclaredFields()).map(f -> f.getName()).sorted().toList()); System.out.println("methods " + Arrays.stream(pc.getDeclaredMethods()).map(m -> m.getName()).sorted().toList()); // 2. which calls reach the handler q.costumes("Hamlet"); q.toString(); q.hashCode(); q.equals(q); q.getClass(); System.out.println("handler saw " + seen); // 3. the class is cached per loader and per ordered interface list Object again = Proxy.newProxyInstance(app, new Class<?>[]{Wardrobe.class}, (p, m, a) -> 0); Object ab = Proxy.newProxyInstance(app, new Class<?>[]{Wardrobe.class, Audited.class}, h); Object ba = Proxy.newProxyInstance(app, new Class<?>[]{Audited.class, Wardrobe.class}, h); System.out.println("same class for the same interface: " + (again.getClass() == pc)); System.out.println("{Wardrobe, Audited} -> " + ab.getClass().getName() + ", {Audited, Wardrobe} -> " + ba.getClass().getName()); } }

alt.title: ProxyAnatomy.kt
alt.html: package workbench.bytecode.l04 import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler import java.lang.reflect.Modifier import java.lang.reflect.Proxy interface KWardrobe { fun costumes(role: String): Int fun dressed(role: String): Boolean = costumes(role) > 0 // a JVM default method (jvmTarget 21) } interface KAudited { fun auditId(): String } /** What Proxy.newProxyInstance generates, which calls reach the handler, and how the class is cached. */ fun main() { val seen = mutableListOf<String>() val h = InvocationHandler { proxy, m, a -> seen += "${m.declaringClass.simpleName}.${m.name}" when (m.name) { "costumes" -> 3 "hashCode" -> 42 "equals" -> proxy === a[0] "toString" -> "KWardrobe proxy" else -> null } } val app = KWardrobe::class.java.classLoader val q = Proxy.newProxyInstance(app, arrayOf(KWardrobe::class.java), h) as KWardrobe // 1. the generated class val pc = q.javaClass println("class ${Modifier.toString(pc.modifiers)} ${pc.name}") println("extends ${pc.superclass.name}, implements ${pc.interfaces.toList()}") println("module ${pc.module.name}, hidden: ${pc.isHidden}") println("fields ${pc.declaredFields.map { it.name }.sorted()}") println("methods ${pc.declaredMethods.map { it.name }.sorted()}") // 2. which calls reach the handler q.costumes("Hamlet") q.toString() q.hashCode() q.equals(q) q.javaClass println("handler saw $seen") // 3. the class is cached per loader and per ordered interface list val again = Proxy.newProxyInstance(app, arrayOf(KWardrobe::class.java)) { _, _, _ -> 0 } val ab = Proxy.newProxyInstance(app, arrayOf(KWardrobe::class.java, KAudited::class.java), h) val ba = Proxy.newProxyInstance(app, arrayOf(KAudited::class.java, KWardrobe::class.java), h) println("same class for the same interface: ${again.javaClass == pc}") println("{KWardrobe, KAudited} -> ${ab.javaClass.name}, {KAudited, KWardrobe} -> ${ba.javaClass.name}") }

try.expect: public final jdk.proxy1.$Proxy0, extending java.lang.reflect.Proxy in module jdk.proxy1, with fields m0 to m4. The handler saw Wardrobe.costumes, Object.toString, Object.hashCode and Object.equals, but not getClass(). The same interface again gives the same class. The two orderings give $Proxy1 and $Proxy2, because the class implements its interfaces in the order you list them, so the cache keys on the order too.

video.title: A dynamic proxy: every call becomes one invoke with a Method and an Object array

sections.h: What reaches the handler, and what the handler owes the caller
sections.html:
Three methods of Object reach the handler: hashCode, equals and toString, each with method.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class. The other public Object methods, such as getClass, wait and notify, are final, and the proxy doesn't override them. The stand-in can't lie about which class it is. For hashCode and other methods with no parameters, args is null, not an empty array.

What you do with equals matters. The company keeps its big props in a store across town, and the show program reaches it through an interface PropStore. The tempting handler for it forwards everything:

Java
InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, args) -> m.invoke(target, args);   // equals too
Kotlin
val h = InvocationHandler { _, m, args -> m.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) }   // equals too

Now proxy.equals(proxy) asks target.equals(proxy). The real prop store has never heard of the proxy, so the answer is false. Ask the proxy whether it is itself, and it says no. The ObjectMethodsDemo shows what that costs:

p.equals(p): false   (target.equals(p) was asked)
listeners.remove(p) after listeners.add(p): false, size still 1
HashSet.contains(p): true   (HashMap checks == before equals)

After listeners.add(p), listeners.remove(p) returns false, and the proxy stays in the list. A HashSet happens to survive, because HashMap compares references with == before it calls equals. That's luck, not correctness.

Here the stand-in picture breaks, and it breaks on identity. Ask a human stand-in "are you the one I gave my note to?", and they answer for themselves. A careless handler passes even that question on to the actor. So answer equals and hashCode by the proxy's own identity (proxy == args[0], System.identityHashCode(proxy)), or decide on purpose how two proxies compare.

The handler also owes the caller the right exceptions. The generated method rethrows unchecked exceptions and the checked exceptions its interface method declares, and wraps any other checked exception in UndeclaredThrowableException. Method.invoke adds a second layer of its own: whatever the target throws arrives wrapped in InvocationTargetException. A handler must catch that and rethrow e.getCause(). Otherwise the caller sees an UndeclaredThrowableException, wrapping an InvocationTargetException, wrapping the real error.

Kotlin makes the first rule easy to trip over. Kotlin has no checked exceptions (exceptions the compiler makes you catch or declare), so a Kotlin interface method declares none unless you write @Throws. A Kotlin implementation may still throw IOException, from a Java library it calls, because Kotlin doesn't check. A handler that unwraps correctly then produces UndeclaredThrowableException, and a Kotlin catch (e: IOException) around the call never matches. The demo's status() shows it. Add @Throws(IOException::class) to interface methods whose implementations can throw checked exceptions.

Two more rules from the Javadoc. Only interfaces can be proxied: passing a class fails with IllegalArgumentException: ... is not an interface. And if two interfaces declare the same method, the handler gets the Method from the first interface in your list, whichever one the caller used.

Answer equals and hashCode by the proxy's identity, and unwrap InvocationTargetException.

Object methods and exceptions are two of the special cases. The third hides in plain sight: default methods.

try.title: Break equals, then the exception contract
steps: Run ObjectMethodsDemo (or the Kotlin twin) and read its five lines.

In forwardingEverything, answer equals before the try: if (m.getName().equals("equals")) return proxy == args[0]; (in Kotlin, rename the lambda's first parameter from _ to proxy, then add if (m.name == "equals") return@newProxyInstance proxy === args[0]). Run it again.
In the Kotlin twin, remove @Throws(IOException::class) from fetch and predict what the catch (e: IOException) block does now. Run it.

code.title: ObjectMethodsDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l04; import java.io.IOException; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.lang.reflect.UndeclaredThrowableException; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; /** Two handler bugs: forwarding equals to the target, and throwing a checked exception the method doesn't declare. */ public class ObjectMethodsDemo { public interface PropStore { String fetch(String prop) throws IOException; // declares IOException String status(); // declares nothing } static class RealPropStore implements PropStore { public String fetch(String prop) throws IOException { throw new IOException("prop store took longer than 120 ms"); } public String status() { return "OPEN"; } } static PropStore forwardingEverything(PropStore target) { return (PropStore) Proxy.newProxyInstance(PropStore.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{PropStore.class}, (proxy, m, args) -> { try { return m.invoke(target, args); // equals and hashCode go to the target too } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); } }); } public static void main(String[] args) { PropStore p = forwardingEverything(new RealPropStore()); System.out.println("p.equals(p): " + p.equals(p) + " (target.equals(p) was asked)"); List<PropStore> listeners = new ArrayList<>(); listeners.add(p); System.out.println("listeners.remove(p) after listeners.add(p): " + listeners.remove(p) + ", size still " + listeners.size()); Set<PropStore> set = new HashSet<>(listeners); System.out.println("HashSet.contains(p): " + set.contains(p) + " (HashMap checks == before equals)"); try { p.fetch("crown"); } catch (IOException e) { System.out.println("declared IOException passes through: " + e.getMessage()); } PropStore angry = (PropStore) Proxy.newProxyInstance(PropStore.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{PropStore.class}, (proxy, m, a) -> { throw new IOException("connection reset"); }); try { angry.status(); } catch (UndeclaredThrowableException e) { System.out.println("undeclared IOException from status() -> UndeclaredThrowableException, cause: " + e.getCause()); } } }

alt.title: ObjectMethodsDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.bytecode.l04 import java.io.IOException import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException import java.lang.reflect.Proxy import java.lang.reflect.UndeclaredThrowableException interface KPropStore { @Throws(IOException::class) fun fetch(prop: String): String // @Throws writes `throws IOException` into the class file fun status(): String // Kotlin declares nothing unless you say so } class RealKPropStore : KPropStore { override fun fetch(prop: String): String = throw IOException("prop store took longer than 120 ms") override fun status() = "OPEN" } fun forwardingEverything(target: KPropStore): KPropStore = Proxy.newProxyInstance(KPropStore::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(KPropStore::class.java)) { _, m, args -> try { m.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) // equals and hashCode go to the target too } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! } } as KPropStore /** Two handler bugs: forwarding equals to the target, and throwing a checked exception the method doesn't declare. */ fun main() { val p = forwardingEverything(RealKPropStore()) println("p.equals(p): ${p.equals(p)} (target.equals(p) was asked)") val listeners = ArrayList<KPropStore>() listeners += p println("listeners.remove(p) after listeners.add(p): ${listeners.remove(p)}, size still ${listeners.size}") val set = HashSet(listeners) println("HashSet.contains(p): ${p in set} (HashMap checks == before equals)") try { p.fetch("crown") } catch (e: IOException) { println("declared IOException passes through: ${e.message}") } val angry = Proxy.newProxyInstance(KPropStore::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(KPropStore::class.java)) { _, _, _ -> throw IOException("connection reset") } as KPropStore try { angry.status() } catch (e: UndeclaredThrowableException) { println("undeclared IOException from status() -> UndeclaredThrowableException, cause: ${e.cause}") } }

try.expect: First run: p.equals(p): false, listeners.remove(p) ... false, size still 1, HashSet.contains(p): true, the declared IOException passing through (prop store took longer than 120 ms), and UndeclaredThrowableException for status(). After the equals fix, p.equals(p) is true, remove returns true and the list is empty (so the set built from it is empty too). Without @Throws, the Kotlin fetch call ends the program with an UndeclaredThrowableException whose cause is the IOException: the catch no longer matches.

sections.h: Default methods: the handler decides who this is
sections.html:
Decorator and Proxy showed the self-invocation trap. The real stockroom's pickBoth called pick through this, and this was the real object, so the proxy never saw the inner calls. Self-invocation is a method calling another method of the same object through this. In the theatre, it's the actor talking to themselves: nothing passes the stage door. Default methods give you a choice about it.

Scenes is the interface the show program uses to ask how long a scene runs. It has an abstract minutes(scene) and a default method total(a, b) that calls minutes twice, on this. If the handler forwards total with method.invoke(target, args), the default body runs on the target. Its this is the target, and its two inner calls skip the proxy. DefaultMethodsDemo logs [total].

JDK 16 added InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, args). It runs the interface's default body with this set to the proxy, so every call the body makes comes back through the handler:

Java
if (method.isDefault()) {
    return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, args);   // the body runs with this = proxy
}
Kotlin
if (method.isDefault) {
    return@InvocationHandler InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, *(args ?: emptyArray()))
}

Now the demo logs [total, minutes, minutes]. The proxy doesn't even need a target. A handler that answers the abstract methods itself, and sends default methods to invokeDefault, is a complete implementation. The demo's target-less proxy answers 5 for every scene, and total comes out at 10. Calling invokeDefault on an abstract method throws IllegalArgumentException, and on a default method your code isn't allowed to reach, it throws IllegalAccessException.

Kotlin interfaces work too. With the labs' JVM target 21, kotlinc 2.4.21 compiles an interface function that has a body to a real JVM default method, plus a DefaultImpls class for older callers. method.isDefault is true, and invokeDefault runs the Kotlin body: the Kotlin twin prints the same three calls.

This choice decides whether a retry proxy is safe, a proxy that calls again when a call fails. The theatre's seat booking runs on another computer, reached through an interface SeatDesk. hold(show, guest) keeps a seat aside for a guest, confirm(holdId) confirms it, and a default method does both: return confirm(hold(show, guest));.

Suppose your handler treats holdAndConfirm like any other method and retries it when it fails. The first attempt holds a seat, then the confirmation fails, so the handler retries the whole method, and the second attempt holds a second seat. Run default methods through invokeDefault and retry only the abstract calls inside them. A failed confirmation is then retried as a confirmation, and the hold that already worked stays at one. The lab tests exactly this.

Run default methods with invokeDefault. Never retry one as a whole.

That's the handler's logic complete. What's left is the price: of making the class, and of every call through it.

try.title: Count the handler calls
steps: Read DefaultMethodsDemo. Predict the handler saw list for both runs, and the total for the target-less proxy.
Change RealScenes.minutes to throw IllegalStateException for "duel" and run it again. What does the first run's log hold when it fails?

code.title: DefaultMethodsDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l04; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException; import java.lang.reflect.Method; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Who is `this` inside a default method? It decides which inner calls the handler sees. */ public class DefaultMethodsDemo { public interface Scenes { int minutes(String scene); default int total(String a, String b) { // calls minutes twice, on `this` return minutes(a) + minutes(b); } } static class RealScenes implements Scenes { public int minutes(String scene) { return scene.length() * 10; } } /** Logs every call it sees. Default methods go either to the target or through invokeDefault. */ static Scenes logging(Scenes target, boolean useInvokeDefault, List<String> log) { InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, args) -> { log.add(m.getName()); if (useInvokeDefault && m.isDefault()) { return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, args); // the body runs with this = proxy } try { return m.invoke(target, args); // the body runs with this = target } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); } }; return (Scenes) Proxy.newProxyInstance(Scenes.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{Scenes.class}, h); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { List<String> log = new ArrayList<>(); int t = logging(new RealScenes(), false, log).total("prologue", "duel"); System.out.println("forward to target: total=" + t + ", handler saw " + log); log.clear(); t = logging(new RealScenes(), true, log).total("prologue", "duel"); System.out.println("invokeDefault: total=" + t + ", handler saw " + log); // no implementation class at all: the handler answers minutes, the interface supplies total Scenes noTarget = (Scenes) Proxy.newProxyInstance(Scenes.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{Scenes.class}, (proxy, m, a) -> m.isDefault() ? InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, a) : 5); System.out.println("no target: total=" + noTarget.total("x", "y")); try { Method abstractOne = Scenes.class.getMethod("minutes", String.class); InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(noTarget, abstractOne, "x"); } catch (Throwable e) { System.out.println("invokeDefault on an abstract method -> " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()); } } }

alt.title: DefaultMethodsDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.bytecode.l04 import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException import java.lang.reflect.Proxy interface KScenes { fun minutes(scene: String): Int fun total(a: String, b: String): Int = // calls minutes twice, on `this` minutes(a) + minutes(b) } class RealKScenes : KScenes { override fun minutes(scene: String) = scene.length * 10 } /** Logs every call it sees. Default methods go either to the target or through invokeDefault. */ fun logging(target: KScenes, useInvokeDefault: Boolean, log: MutableList<String>): KScenes = Proxy.newProxyInstance(KScenes::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(KScenes::class.java)) { proxy, m, args -> log += m.name if (useInvokeDefault && m.isDefault) { InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, *args) // the body runs with this = proxy } else { try { m.invoke(target, *args) // the body runs with this = target } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! } } } as KScenes /** Who is `this` inside a default method? It decides which inner calls the handler sees. */ fun main() { val log = mutableListOf<String>() var t = logging(RealKScenes(), false, log).total("prologue", "duel") println("forward to target: total=$t, handler saw $log") log.clear() t = logging(RealKScenes(), true, log).total("prologue", "duel") println("invokeDefault: total=$t, handler saw $log") // no implementation class at all: the handler answers minutes, the interface supplies total val noTarget = Proxy.newProxyInstance(KScenes::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(KScenes::class.java)) { proxy, m, a -> if (m.isDefault) InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, *a) else 5 } as KScenes println("no target: total=${noTarget.total("x", "y")}") try { InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(noTarget, KScenes::class.java.getMethod("minutes", String::class.java), "x") } catch (e: Throwable) { println("invokeDefault on an abstract method -> ${e.javaClass.simpleName}") } }

try.expect: forward to target: total=120, handler saw [total], then invokeDefault: total=120, handler saw [total, minutes, minutes], then no target: total=10 (two answers of 5), then IllegalArgumentException. With the exception for "duel", the program stops in the first run. Its stack trace shows RealScenes.minutes called from Scenes.total on the target, and the handler never logged a minutes call: a retry or a timer in the handler couldn't have seen the failing call. In the invokeDefault version, the same failure would pass through the handler as the second minutes call.

sections.h: One class per loader and interface list, and a few nanoseconds per call
sections.html:
Generating a class is the expensive part, and the JDK does it only once. Proxy caches proxy classes per class loader, keyed by the ordered list of interfaces. Ten thousand newProxyInstance calls with the same loader and interfaces generate one class and construct ten thousand small objects. Listing the same interfaces in a different order generates a second class, as ProxyAnatomy showed with $Proxy1 and $Proxy2.

Each class loader gets one dynamic module for its proxies, a module the JDK creates while the program runs. On the runs for this track, proxies for app-loader interfaces landed in jdk.proxy1, and a Runnable proxy created with the bootstrap loader (null) landed in jdk.proxy2. If any interface isn't public, the proxy class goes into that interface's package instead, and isn't public either (demo.$Proxy8 in one run). Calling Constructor.newInstance on a proxy class in a dynamic module throws IllegalAccessException. Use newProxyInstance, because Proxy.getProxyClass is deprecated.

The cost of each call is the bytecode from the first section: an Object[], boxing, a call to the handler, and whatever the handler does. JMH, the JDK project's tool for timing small pieces of code, measured add(3, 4) four ways on JDK 25. This was one run on a shared 4-core machine, with one fork (one separate JVM run) and wide error bars:

Call ns per call
direct 0.83
Byte Buddy subclass with @SuperCall (lesson 5) 0.88
JDK proxy, handler calls method.invoke(target, args) 4.3
plain Method.invoke with boxing 11.8

Read the order, not the decimals. A few nanoseconds per call is nothing next to a 120 ms call to the seat desk on another computer. It does show up in a loop that calls a proxied interface millions of times, and there a subclass proxy or plain code wins.

You can save the generated class and read it yourself. -Djdk.proxy.ProxyGenerator.saveGeneratedFiles=true writes it to jdk/proxy1/$Proxy0.class under the current folder. On JDK 21 that just works. On the JDK 24 to 27 builds tested for this track, JDK 25 included, the JDK writes the first file, and then newProxyInstance throws NullPointerException. The JDK source explains it: a return null; that used to sit inside a doPrivileged block now returns from generateProxyClass itself. The file is still written, so you can read it on any of them.

Here's the limit of today's tool, and it's a hard one. A JDK proxy can only implement interfaces. A class with no interface, or a Kotlin class that is final by default, can't have a stand-in this way at all.

try.title: Read the class the JDK wrote
steps: Run ProxyAnatomy once with Gradle so its classes exist. Then, from labs/, run the commands below. They work in a temporary folder, because the flag writes into the current one.
On JDK 24 or later, expect a NullPointerException after the first file is written. Carry on with javap.
Find costumes and compare it with the listing in the first section. Then find the static initializer: where does it look up m3?

code.title: terminal
code.html: D=$PWD/bytecode/build/classes/java/demo cd "$(mktemp -d)" java -Djdk.proxy.ProxyGenerator.saveGeneratedFiles=true -cp "$D" workbench.bytecode.l04.ProxyAnatomy javap -c -p 'jdk/proxy1/$Proxy0.class' | less

try.expect: costumes loads h, the proxy and m3, builds a one-element Object[], calls InvocationHandler.invoke, then runs checkcast Integer and intValue. The static initializer calls Class.getMethod for hashCode, equals, toString, costumes and dressed, and stores them in m0 to m4. For the interface's methods, it first finds Wardrobe by name with Class.forName(name, false, loader); JDK 21 does that for Object too. On JDK 21 the program also prints its normal output. On JDK 24 and later, it stops with the NullPointerException after writing $Proxy0.class.

compare.title: A tracing proxy in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Tracing.java
java.html: @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") static <T> T tracing(Class<T> iface, T target, List<String> log) { InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, args) -> { if (m.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class) { // 1. identity, not the target's return switch (m.getName()) { case "equals" -> proxy == args[0]; case "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy); default -> "Tracing[" + target + "]"; }; } log.add(m.getName()); if (m.isDefault()) return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, args); // 2. this = proxy try { return m.invoke(target, args); // 3. args is null for no-arg methods } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); // 4. the target's own exception } }; return (T) Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, h); }

kotlin.title: Tracing.kt
kotlin.html: inline fun <reified T : Any> tracing(target: T, log: MutableList<String>): T = Proxy.newProxyInstance(T::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(T::class.java)) { proxy, m, args -> val a = args ?: emptyArray() // 3. null for no-arg methods when { m.declaringClass == Any::class.java -> when (m.name) { // 1. identity "equals" -> proxy === a[0] "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy) else -> "Tracing[$target]" } else -> { log += m.name if (m.isDefault) InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, *a) // 2. this = proxy else try { m.invoke(target, *a) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! // 4. the target's own exception } } } } as T

compare.note: Same JVM mechanism, same four cases. The Kotlin version is shorter because reified T reads T::class.java itself, so callers write tracing(desk, log). Two Kotlin-specific traps sit in it. args is a nullable Java array, null for methods with no parameters, so spreading it directly (*args) throws NullPointerException on hashCode(). And Kotlin interfaces declare no checked exceptions unless you add @Throws, so an IOException from a Java library, which the handler rethrows correctly, still reaches Kotlin callers as UndeclaredThrowableException.

worked.title: A test double for SeatDesk with no implementation class

steps.say: A test needs a SeatDesk that returns canned answers and records what was called, and you don't want to write a class with every method. A test double is a stand-in built for a test. A proxy with no target can be one. Start with the cases every handler needs.
steps.code: static SeatDesk fakeDesk(Map<String, Object> answers, List<String> calls) { InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, args) -> { // 1. Object methods: identity, so the fake behaves in collections if (m.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class) { return switch (m.getName()) { case "equals" -> proxy == args[0]; case "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy); default -> "FakeDesk" + answers.keySet(); }; } // 2. default methods: run the real interface body, which calls back through this handler if (m.isDefault()) return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, args); // 3. abstract methods: record the call and return the canned answer calls.add(m.getName() + Arrays.toString(args)); if (!answers.containsKey(m.getName())) throw new UnsupportedOperationException(m.getName()); return answers.get(m.getName()); }; return (SeatDesk) Proxy.newProxyInstance( SeatDesk.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{SeatDesk.class}, h); }

alt.html: fun fakeDesk(answers: Map<String, Any>, calls: MutableList<String>): SeatDesk = Proxy.newProxyInstance(SeatDesk::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(SeatDesk::class.java)) { proxy, m, args -> val a = args ?: emptyArray() when { // 1. Object methods: identity, so the fake behaves in collections m.declaringClass == Any::class.java -> when (m.name) { "equals" -> proxy === a[0] "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy) else -> "FakeDesk${answers.keys}" } // 2. default methods: run the real interface body, which calls back through this handler m.isDefault -> InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, *a) // 3. abstract methods: record the call and return the canned answer else -> { calls += m.name + a.contentToString() answers[m.name] ?: throw UnsupportedOperationException(m.name) } } } as SeatDesk

steps.say: Use it. The interesting call is the default method: the fake has no code for holdAndConfirm, yet the interface's own body runs, and its two inner calls are recorded in order. A run of this code printed confirmed hold-hamlet [hold[Hamlet, ana], confirm[hold-hamlet]]. That works only because of invokeDefault: forwarding to a target isn't possible here, since there is no target.
steps.code: List<String> calls = new ArrayList<>(); SeatDesk desk = fakeDesk( Map.of("hold", "hold-hamlet", "confirm", "confirmed hold-hamlet"), calls); String result = desk.holdAndConfirm("Hamlet", "ana"); // 4. exercise the default assertThat(result).isEqualTo("confirmed hold-hamlet"); assertThat(calls).containsExactly("hold[Hamlet, ana]", "confirm[hold-hamlet]");

alt.html: val calls = mutableListOf<String>() val desk = fakeDesk(mapOf("hold" to "hold-hamlet", "confirm" to "confirmed hold-hamlet"), calls) val result = desk.holdAndConfirm("Hamlet", "ana") // 4. exercise the default assertThat(result).isEqualTo("confirmed hold-hamlet") assertThat(calls).containsExactly("hold[Hamlet, ana]", "confirm[hold-hamlet]")

steps.say: Check the edges before you trust it. A canned answer of the wrong type fails at the proxy's checkcast, with a ClassCastException from the generated method rather than from your handler. A missing answer for a method returning int would be null, and the proxy's unboxing would turn that into a NullPointerException, so the handler throws a clear UnsupportedOperationException instead. And this fake works for one interface only. Mocking libraries, which build test doubles for you, grow the same idea with argument matchers and support for classes.

lab.title: A retrying, timing proxy for the seat desk
steps: Run the tests once. All seven fail. Read SeatDesk and the FakeDesk in the test: it fails a scripted number of calls and counts every one. RetryPolicy says how many attempts a call gets and which failures are worth another try, and CallRecorder receives one line per finished call.
In ResilientProxy.wrap, create the proxy with Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, handler) and return iface.cast(...).
Write the handler's first two cases: Object methods answered by identity and "Resilient[" + target + "]", then default methods through InvocationHandler.invokeDefault.

Write the retry loop: read the clock once, call method.invoke(target, args), and on InvocationTargetException take getCause(). Try again while attempts are left and policy.retries(cause) is true. Record iface.getSimpleName() + "." + method.getName() with the attempt count and end - start once, when the call ends.
Run the tests until all seven pass. Then read defaultMethodShellIsNotRetried and say out loud why the desk saw one hold.
hints: The order of the cases matters. equals is not a default method, but check Object methods first anyway, so nothing else ever sees them.
The fake clock moves 5 ms per read. If the recorded time isn't 5ms, you're reading the clock more than twice per call.

throw cause; compiles because InvocationHandler.invoke is declared throws Throwable. Because the cause is the target's own exception, the generated method lets DeskUnavailableException through: hold declares it.

drill.title: The four cases from memory
drill.prompt: Close the page. Write an InvocationHandler that times each call of an interface and reports the method name, handling the four cases in the right order: Object methods, default methods, the timed call, and exceptions. Then check your version against the answer. Which case did you forget?

answer.html: InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, args) -> { if (m.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class) { // 1. Object methods return switch (m.getName()) { case "equals" -> proxy == args[0]; case "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy); default -> "Timed[" + target + "]"; }; } if (m.isDefault()) return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, args); // 2. defaults: this = proxy long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { return m.invoke(target, args); // 3. the timed call } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); // 4. unwrap } finally { timings.record(m.getName(), System.nanoTime() - t0); } };

alt.html: val h = InvocationHandler { proxy, m, args -> val a = args ?: emptyArray() if (m.declaringClass == Any::class.java) { // 1. Object methods return@InvocationHandler when (m.name) { "equals" -> proxy === a[0] "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy) else -> "Timed[$target]" } } if (m.isDefault) return@InvocationHandler InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, *a) // 2. defaults val t0 = System.nanoTime() try { m.invoke(target, *a) // 3. the timed call } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! // 4. unwrap } finally { timings.record(m.name, System.nanoTime() - t0) } }

recap: Proxy.newProxyInstance generates a public final $ProxyN extends Proxy that implements exactly your interfaces, in order. Each method boxes its arguments into an Object[] and calls h.invoke(proxy, Method, args).
hashCode, equals and toString reach the handler; getClass doesn't. Answer equals and hashCode by the proxy's identity, or collections can't find the proxy.

Unchecked exceptions and declared checked exceptions pass through; any other checked exception becomes UndeclaredThrowableException. Unwrap InvocationTargetException, and use @Throws on Kotlin interfaces.

InvocationHandler.invokeDefault (JDK 16) runs a default body with this = proxy, so its inner calls come back through the handler. Never retry a default method as a whole: retry the abstract calls inside it.
Proxy classes are cached per loader and ordered interface list, in one jdk.proxyN module per loader. A call costs a few nanoseconds: nothing next to a network call, visible in tight loops.
The limit: a JDK proxy can only implement interfaces. A class with no interface, or a final Kotlin class, can't be wrapped this way.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to wrap every client of a remote service in a JDK proxy that retries on timeouts. Explain what the JDK generates, the four cases their handler must handle, and the one retry rule that keeps a default method like holdAndConfirm from holding two seats.
explain.answer: Proxy.newProxyInstance generates one final class per class loader and interface list. Each of its methods boxes the arguments into an Object[] and calls the handler with the proxy and a cached Method. The handler must first answer equals, hashCode and toString itself, by the proxy's identity, or collections stop finding the proxy. Second, it must run default methods with InvocationHandler.invokeDefault, so the body runs with this as the proxy and each inner call comes back through the handler. Third, it calls the target with method.invoke and retries only the failures the policy names, such as a timeout. Fourth, it rethrows InvocationTargetException.getCause(), so callers get the service's own exception and not an UndeclaredThrowableException. The retry rule: never retry a default method as one unit. Retry the abstract calls inside it, so a failed confirm is retried as a confirm, and the hold that already worked isn't sent again.

deeper.html:
Three corners of Proxy that the lesson skipped.

Modules and visibility. If every interface is public and in an exported package, the proxy class is public, in an unconditionally exported but non-open package of a dynamic module. If any interface isn't public, the proxy class isn't public either, and goes into that interface's package and module, so all non-public interfaces must share one package. If an interface is in a package its module doesn't export, the proxy goes into a non-exported package of a dynamic module. In every dynamic-module case, Constructor.newInstance on the proxy class throws IllegalAccessException, which is why Proxy.getProxyClass is deprecated.

What can fail at creation. newProxyInstance throws IllegalArgumentException when an element isn't a non-hidden, non-sealed interface, when an interface appears twice, when an interface isn't visible by name through the loader you pass (Class.forName(i.getName(), false, loader) != i), when two interfaces have a method with the same signature and incompatible return types, or when you pass more than 65,535 interfaces. The loader rule is the one you'll meet: in a plugin system or a test runner, pass the loader that defined the interface (iface.getClassLoader()), not some other loader that holds a second copy of it (lesson 1).

The caches. Proxy keeps the constructors in a ClassLoaderValue, so the cache entry goes away with the loader. A second cache backs isProxyClass. And a ClassValue of ConcurrentHashMap<Method, MethodHandle> holds the method handles behind invokeDefault, so only the first call of each default method pays for the lookup.

The saveGeneratedFiles crash from the last section is easy to see in the source. At jdk-21-ga, generateProxyClass wrote the file inside AccessController.doPrivileged(new PrivilegedAction<>() { ... return null; }), and that return null belonged to the inner block. At jdk-24-ga, the release that permanently disabled the Security Manager, the doPrivileged wrapper is gone, and the same return null; now returns from generateProxyClass itself, so defineClass receives null bytes. That matches the message JDK 25 printed: Cannot read the array length because "b" is null.
